paras: The Helena election-day violence took place at the Phillips County courthouse in Helena, Arkansas, on September 4, 1882, when Democrats and deputy sheriffs beat Republican ticket distributors and drove a crowd of about 1,000 Black voters from the polls. A deputy sheriff fired three times at a Black man, few Black men voted, and the Democrats claimed the county. Republican papers across the North treated the episode as the worst case of "bulldozing" in the state election, while Democratic papers dismissed it as invention.

According to the Detroit Post, Democratic county judge Sanders had arranged the precincts so that about 1,300 voters, nearly all Republicans and mostly Black, had to travel ten or twelve miles to vote at the courthouse. Republicans had put up no county ticket in 1878 or 1880 but ran one in 1882 after Governor Churchill asked that they be allowed a fair vote and local Democrats pledged there would be no intimidation. Expecting the judges to hide the count, Republicans prepared ballots with detachable coupons so that their distributors could keep a record of each Republican vote.

Gen. M. L. Stephenson, a former state supreme court judge, telegraphed that the courthouse "was taken last night, locked and guarded" and that judges were chosen inside with no one outside allowed to take part. The polls opened at 7:45 a.m., with ballots passed through a hole high in a door so that voters could not see the box.

About an hour later, a Globe-Democrat correspondent wrote, several whites came out of the building, seized a distributor at the south door, took his coupons, struck him on the head and kicked him twice, and the same was done at the other door. Deputy sheriffs and others, "some flourishing their revolvers," then moved through the crowd ordering it to disperse, and within half an hour few of the 1,000 or more Black voters were within half a mile. Stephenson reported that a deputy sheriff shot at a Black man three times and that this frightened the others from voting, while the Memphis Avalanche's Helena special said simply that "One negro was shot."

The Avalanche named John Q. Taylor, the Republican candidate for county clerk, along with Judge Bennett and Jacob Triber, as men abused at the courthouse, made to give up their tickets and told to go home. A letter later published by Congressman W. R. Moore said Taylor, an old man who had lived in Helena for thirty-four years, "was literally kicked from the Court House."

Few Black voters returned, and the Springfield Republican reported that the Republican managers abandoned the contest. The Globe-Democrat said Democrats counted a majority of 1,400 in a county where Garfield had led by 1,443 two years earlier, and that its correspondent was told to leave and spent the night in another state. A Democratic dispatch reported one arrest without naming the person, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial over the shooting or the assaults appears in the coverage.

The first word reached the country through the Avalanche's Helena special, carried by Western papers on September 5 and 8 under heads such as "Model Election," and through a Little Rock dispatch printed in the Huntsville Gazette. Republican papers in Massachusetts, Maine, Ohio and Michigan built editorials on the Globe-Democrat's reports through October, the Portland Daily Press listing Helena's "intimidation" first among four Arkansas methods of taking Republican votes. A Sacramento editorial on the lynching of Jack Turner in Alabama added that at the Arkansas election Republican voters were driven from the polls "and a negro was billed [killed]," without naming a town.

Democratic papers answered that the stories were fabricated: the Arkansaw Democrat's Helena correspondent warned readers against the Globe-Democrat's "false and slanderous charges of bulldozing," and the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, reprinted in Arkansas, mocked its "Arkansas Outrage Mill." A Missouri Democratic weekly went further, saying that any thousand men who let a hundred drive them from the polls were "not wothy of suflerage." The Memphis Public Ledger reprinted the Little Rock Gazette's interview with the Democratic county chairman under the head "Running Down Slanders."

The Democratic accounts differ on nearly every point: the Arkansaw Democrat's Helena dispatch said the election was quiet, that 88 "colored cavalry" under Jack Corbin had tried to take the polls, and that the coupon workers were ejected by the sheriff and deputies with no injury. Judge L. H. Mangum, the Democratic county chairman, conceded that deputies "forcibly ejected" Taylor when he refused to stop collecting coupons but said no Republican was kept from voting. Mangum blamed the lost vote on Republican leaders, saying S. D. Lewis kept hundreds of Black men waiting at the telegraph office for a second ballot box the Governor never ordered.
The fate of the man fired on is also unsettled: Stephenson said he was shot at, the Avalanche that he was shot, and only the Sacramento editorial spoke of a death.

reader.title: Helena election-day violence (1882)
bases: Deputy sheriffs and Democrats beat Republican ticket distributors and, with revolvers drawn, drove a crowd of about 1,000 Black voters from the Helena courthouse polls (A22, A32, A9).

Stephenson's telegram, the Avalanche special and the Globe-Democrat correspondent agree on assaults, a shooting and the dispersal (A9, A2, A32), and Mangum admits deputies forcibly ejected Taylor (A21), but the Arkansaw Democrat's Helena dispatch calls the election quiet and denies any injury or denial of the vote (A10).

accounts.label: Stephenson's telegram / Little Rock dispatch
accounts.gist: Bulldozers held the locked courthouse overnight, chose the judges inside, knocked down ticket distributors and drove voters off; a deputy sheriff shot at a colored man three times, and no voting took place after 9 o'clock.

accounts.label: Memphis Avalanche Helena special
accounts.gist: The election was carried by bulldozing; one Black man was shot, and Taylor, Bennett and Triber were abused and made to give up tickets.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat correspondent
accounts.gist: Whites from the building seized, robbed, struck and kicked the coupon distributors at both doors; deputy sheriffs and others, some flourishing revolvers, then dispersed the crowd of 1,000 or more Black voters.

accounts.label: Arkansaw Democrat Helena special
accounts.gist: The election was quiet with one arrest; 88 colored cavalry under Jack Corbin tried to seize the polls; the sheriff and deputies ejected the coupon workers without injury, and Republican bosses told Black voters to go home.

accounts.label: Democratic chairman Mangum
accounts.gist: No Republican was kept from voting; Taylor resisted an order to desist and was forcibly ejected by deputies, and Black voters stayed away waiting for a second ballot box their leaders promised.

framing.detail: The Springfield Republican called it a 'specially flagrant case' and an 'outrage'; the Detroit Post headed it 'Bulldozing in Arkansas' and 'shameless Democratic election frauds'.
The Portland Daily Press's 'At Their Old Tricks' named intimidation at Helena the first of four Arkansas methods of stealing Republican votes.
The Arkansaw Democrat dispatch warned readers against the Globe-Democrat's 'false and slanderous charges of bulldozing'.
Fair Play called the reports manufactured to order and said 1,000 men who let 100 drive them off were not worthy of suffrage.
The St. Louis Post-Dispatch, reprinted in Arkansas, mocked the Globe-Democrat's 'Arkansas Outrage Mill' and blamed a Republican faction fight.
Western papers ran the Avalanche wire under 'The Arkansas Election' and 'Model Election'.
